title: Everything about employees
statement: Show every column and every row of the `employees` table.
solution: SELECT * FROM employees;
hints: SELECT chooses columns and FROM chooses the table.
The star * means all columns.
Write SELECT, then the star, then FROM, then the table name.
SELECT * FROM employees;

title: Customer names
statement: Show only the `name` column of the `customers` table.
solution: SELECT name FROM customers;
hints: Name the column instead of using a star.
After SELECT, write the column name you want.
SELECT the name column FROM the customers table.
SELECT name FROM customers;

title: Sales team
statement: Show the `name` and `salary` of employees in the Sales department.
solution: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE department = 'Sales';
hints: WHERE keeps only rows that match a condition.
Text values go in single quotes. A single = compares in SQL.
SELECT the two columns, FROM employees, WHERE department equals Sales.
SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE department = 'Sales';

title: High earners
statement: Show the `name` of every employee who earns more than 70000.
solution: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary > 70000;
hints: You need a comparison on the salary column.
Numbers do not need quotes. The symbol > means greater than.
SELECT name FROM employees, keeping rows WHERE salary is greater than 70000.
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary > 70000;

title: Engineers below 80000
statement: Show the `name` and `salary` of employees who work in Engineering and earn less than 80000.
solution: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE department = 'Engineering' AND salary < 80000;
hints: Two conditions must both be true.
Join the two conditions with AND.
WHERE department equals Engineering AND salary is less than 80000.
SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE department = 'Engineering' AND salary < 80000;

title: Mice and keyboards
statement: Show the `id` and `product` of every order for a Mouse or a Keyboard.
solution: SELECT id, product FROM orders WHERE product IN ('Mouse', 'Keyboard');
hints: You could write two conditions with OR, but there is a shorter way.
IN lets you list several allowed values in brackets.
WHERE product IN, then the two product names in quotes inside brackets.
SELECT id, product FROM orders WHERE product IN ('Mouse', 'Keyboard');

title: Names ending in a
statement: Show the `name` of customers whose name ends with the letter a.
solution: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE name LIKE '%a';
hints: LIKE compares text to a pattern.
In a pattern, the percent sign % stands for any run of characters, including none.
The pattern for ends with a is a percent sign followed by a, in quotes.
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE name LIKE '%a';

title: People without a manager
statement: Show the `name` of employees who have no manager. In the table this means `manager_id` is NULL.
solution: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL;
hints: NULL means a missing value.
You cannot compare with = NULL. There is a special phrase for it.
WHERE manager_id IS NULL.
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL;

title: Mid-priced orders
statement: Show the `id` and `amount` of orders with an amount from 100 to 300, including both 100 and 300.
solution: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount BETWEEN 100 AND 300;
hints: A range with both ends included has a short form.
BETWEEN a AND b includes both a and b.
WHERE amount BETWEEN 100 AND 300.
SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount BETWEEN 100 AND 300;

title: Which cities
statement: Show each city where at least one customer lives, once each, with no repeats.
solution: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers;
hints: Several customers share a city, so a plain SELECT repeats it.
DISTINCT removes repeated rows.
SELECT DISTINCT, then the city column, FROM customers.
SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers;

title: Pay list
statement: Show the `name` and `salary` of every employee, with the highest salary first. If two people earn the same, put the name that comes first alphabetically first.
solution: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC, name;
hints: ORDER BY sorts the result.
DESC means biggest first. Add a second column after a comma to break ties.
ORDER BY salary DESC, then name.
SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC, name;

title: Top three paid
statement: Show the `name` and `salary` of the three highest paid employees, highest first.
solution: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3;
hints: Sort first, then keep only the top rows.
LIMIT 3 keeps the first three rows, and it goes last in the query.
ORDER BY salary DESC, then LIMIT 3.
SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3;

title: Pay inside each department
statement: Show `department`, `name` and `salary` for every employee. Sort by department A to Z. Inside a department, highest salary first, and for equal salaries the name A to Z.
solution: SELECT department, name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY department, salary DESC, name;
hints: You need to sort by three things in order of importance.
List them after ORDER BY, separated by commas. Each can have its own DESC.
ORDER BY department, then salary DESC, then name.
SELECT department, name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY department, salary DESC, name;

title: Newest two hires
statement: Show the `name` and `hire_year` of the two most recently hired employees, newest first.
solution: SELECT name, hire_year FROM employees ORDER BY hire_year DESC LIMIT 2;
hints: Newest means the biggest hire_year.
Sort so the biggest year comes first, then keep two rows.
ORDER BY hire_year DESC LIMIT 2.
SELECT name, hire_year FROM employees ORDER BY hire_year DESC LIMIT 2;

title: Latest orders
statement: Show the `id` and `order_date` of the three most recent orders, newest first. Dates are text written as YYYY-MM-DD, which sort correctly.
solution: SELECT id, order_date FROM orders ORDER BY order_date DESC LIMIT 3;
hints: Dates in this form sort the same way as text.
DESC puts the latest date first.
ORDER BY order_date DESC, then LIMIT 3.
SELECT id, order_date FROM orders ORDER BY order_date DESC LIMIT 3;

title: Two lowest balances
statement: Show the `id` and `balance` of the two accounts with the lowest balance, lowest first.
solution: SELECT id, balance FROM accounts ORDER BY balance ASC LIMIT 2;
hints: Lowest first is the normal sort direction.
ASC is the default, so you may leave it out.
ORDER BY balance, then LIMIT 2.
SELECT id, balance FROM accounts ORDER BY balance ASC LIMIT 2;

title: Orders with customer names
statement: Show the customer `name`, the order `product` and the order `amount` for every order.
solution: SELECT c.name, o.product, o.amount FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;
hints: The customer name lives in a different table from the order.
JOIN customers ON the order's customer_id equals the customer's id.
FROM orders, JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id. Aliases o and c save typing.
SELECT c.name, o.product, o.amount FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;

title: Orders from Austin
statement: Show the customer `name` and the order `product` for orders placed by customers who live in Austin.
solution: SELECT c.name, o.product FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE c.city = 'Austin';
hints: First join, then filter.
After the JOIN, a WHERE can use columns from either table.
Join orders to customers, then WHERE the customer's city equals Austin.
SELECT c.name, o.product FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE c.city = 'Austin';

title: Customers and their accounts
statement: Show the customer `name`, the account `type` and the account `balance` for every account.
solution: SELECT c.name, a.type, a.balance FROM accounts a JOIN customers c ON a.customer_id = c.id;
hints: Accounts hold a customer_id.
Join accounts to customers where the ids match.
FROM accounts, JOIN customers ON accounts.customer_id = customers.id.
SELECT c.name, a.type, a.balance FROM accounts a JOIN customers c ON a.customer_id = c.id;

title: Customers who never ordered
statement: Show the `name` of every customer who has not placed any order.
solution: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;
hints: An ordinary JOIN loses customers with no orders. You need a different kind.
LEFT JOIN keeps every customer, and fills the order columns with NULL when there is no match.
LEFT JOIN orders ON the ids match, then keep rows WHERE the order id IS NULL.
SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;

title: Customers with a return
statement: Show the `name` of each customer who has at least one order with status returned. List each name once.
solution: SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'returned';
hints: A customer with two returned orders would appear twice.
DISTINCT removes repeated rows.
Join customers to orders, keep status returned, and use DISTINCT.
SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'returned';

title: Employee and manager
statement: Show each employee's name as `employee` and their manager's name as `manager`. Leave out employees who have no manager.
solution: SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;
hints: The manager is another row in the same table.
Use the table twice with two different aliases, one for the employee and one for the manager.
Join employees e to employees m where e.manager_id equals m.id.
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;

title: Orders of savers
statement: Show the customer `name` and the order `product` for customers who own a savings account. A customer who owns a savings account and has three orders should give three rows.
solution: SELECT c.name, o.product FROM customers c JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.id JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE a.type = 'savings';
hints: You need three tables: customers, accounts and orders.
A second JOIN can follow the first. Both join back to customers.
customers JOIN accounts ON the ids match, JOIN orders ON the ids match, WHERE the account type equals savings.
SELECT c.name, o.product FROM customers c JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.id JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE a.type = 'savings';

title: Headcount per department
statement: Show each `department` and the number of employees in it, as a column called `headcount`.
solution: SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount FROM employees GROUP BY department;
hints: You want one row per department, not one per employee.
GROUP BY department makes one pile per department. COUNT(*) counts rows in each pile.
SELECT department and COUNT(*) AS headcount, FROM employees, GROUP BY department.
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount FROM employees GROUP BY department;

title: Average pay
statement: Show each `department` and its average salary, rounded to the nearest whole number, as a column called `average_pay`.
solution: SELECT department, ROUND(AVG(salary)) AS average_pay FROM employees GROUP BY department;
hints: AVG works out an average.
ROUND(value) rounds to a whole number. Put AVG inside ROUND.
SELECT department, ROUND(AVG(salary)) AS average_pay, FROM employees, GROUP BY department.
SELECT department, ROUND(AVG(salary)) AS average_pay FROM employees GROUP BY department;

title: Big departments
statement: Show each `department` that has more than 3 employees, with its `headcount`.
solution: SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount FROM employees GROUP BY department HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;
hints: WHERE cannot filter on a count, because the count does not exist until after grouping.
HAVING filters groups, and it comes after GROUP BY.
Group by department, then HAVING COUNT(*) greater than 3.
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount FROM employees GROUP BY department HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;

title: Shipped totals
statement: For orders with status shipped only, show each `customer_id` and the total of their `amount` as `total`.
solution: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped' GROUP BY customer_id;
hints: Filter the rows before you group them.
WHERE comes before GROUP BY. SUM adds up a column.
SELECT customer_id and SUM(amount) AS total, FROM orders, WHERE status equals shipped, GROUP BY customer_id.
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped' GROUP BY customer_id;

title: Big spenders
statement: Show the `name` and total spent (as `total`) for each customer whose orders add up to 1000 or more, counting all orders whatever their status.
solution: SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) AS total FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.name HAVING SUM(o.amount) >= 1000;
hints: You need a join for the name, a group for the totals and a filter on the totals.
Join customers to orders, GROUP BY the name, and use HAVING for the total test.
SELECT name and SUM(amount) AS total, FROM customers JOIN orders, GROUP BY name, HAVING SUM(amount) at least 1000.
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) AS total FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.name HAVING SUM(o.amount) >= 1000;

title: Top pay in each department
statement: Show each `department` and its highest salary, as a column called `top_pay`.
solution: SELECT department, MAX(salary) AS top_pay FROM employees GROUP BY department;
hints: MAX gives the biggest value in a group.
Group by department.
SELECT department and MAX(salary) AS top_pay, FROM employees, GROUP BY department.
SELECT department, MAX(salary) AS top_pay FROM employees GROUP BY department;

title: Orders by status
statement: Show each order `status` and the number of orders with that status, as `n`. Put the status with the most orders first. If two statuses have the same number, put the one that comes first alphabetically first.
solution: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY n DESC, status;
hints: Count per group, then sort the groups.
ORDER BY comes after GROUP BY, and it can use the name you gave with AS.
GROUP BY status, then ORDER BY n DESC, then status.
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY n DESC, status;

title: Account types with a high average
statement: Show each account `type` whose average balance is above 5000, with the average rounded to 2 decimal places as `average_balance`.
solution: SELECT type, ROUND(AVG(balance), 2) AS average_balance FROM accounts GROUP BY type HAVING AVG(balance) > 5000;
hints: The test is on an average, so it belongs in HAVING.
ROUND takes a second value: how many decimal places to keep.
Group by type. HAVING AVG(balance) greater than 5000. SELECT the rounded average.
SELECT type, ROUND(AVG(balance), 2) AS average_balance FROM accounts GROUP BY type HAVING AVG(balance) > 5000;

title: Repeat buyers
statement: Show the `name` of each customer with at least 3 orders, and their number of orders as `n`.
solution: SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS n FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.name HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
hints: You need names from customers and a count from orders.
Join, group by the name, and filter the count with HAVING.
Join customers to orders. GROUP BY name. HAVING COUNT(*) at least 3.
SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS n FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.name HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
